Encoder Anatomy

What a neural audio encoder actually does to a clip — shown on real data: every picture below is VCTK clip p225_004 pushed through the real EnCodec-24k backend on this machine. Nothing is a cartoon.

1 · The chunking: audio becomes a sequence of time slots

The encoder never sees "the clip." A convolutional front-end slides over the waveform and emits one output every 13.3 ms (the hop). Each gold-width slot below becomes exactly one latent vector. A 6-second clip → ~450 slots.

One subtlety: the slot is where the vector lands, not all it saw — the conv stack's receptive field reaches wider than one hop (neighboring slots share context), and that's before any transformer layers. In WavLM every frame sees the entire clip.

2 · Chunking into what: 128 invented axes

A spectrogram chunks time into designed features: energy at 100 Hz, at 200 Hz… axes a human chose. The encoder chunks the same signal into learned features: 128 dimensions that gradient descent invented because they made compression work. No dimension means "frequency" — each is some entangled mixture of pitch, timbre, phonation, noise texture.

Same clip, same time axis. Top: physics you can read. Bottom: the encoding — meaningful to the decoder, alien to us. The pilot's whole bet is that distortions still leave legible geometric tracks in this alien space.

How does one become the other? Not by rotation or relabeling — by nonlinear mixing. Measure it: correlate every mel band with every latent dimension across this clip's 331 frames:

Left: the designed mapping — one band, one frequency region, by construction. Middle: the measured bridge on real data — if latents were just a reshuffled spectrogram you'd see a crisp diagonal; instead every latent dim correlates with many bands and vice versa. Right: three of the strongest dims, each listening across the whole spectrum at once. That entanglement is why probing is a real question — the information survives the mixing (spectrogram→latent loses little), but no single axis "means" anything, so structure must be read geometrically (directions, not coordinates).

3 · One column of that image = one frame vector

The gold column at 1.15 s, pulled out and laid flat: 128 floats. That's the atomic unit — frames[T, D] is just T of these stacked. Real-valued, no phase; "direction" and "length" are the only geometry it has.

4 · Damage photographed in latent space

Same clip, crackled (dropout severity 5 — zeroed micro-bursts), re-encoded. Subtract the clean latent:

The |difference| panel is Δ before pooling: damage shows up as vertical stripes exactly where bursts hit — localized in time, smeared across all 128 dims. Pool it over time and you get the clip-level shift vector Δ whose direction should say "dropout" and whose length should say "severity 5." That's the experiment.

5 · Depth taps and the final pooling

Codecs quantize z through stacked codebooks (RVQ): d1 keeps only the coarsest description; d8 adds seven refinement layers. The sweep asks at which depth damage information survives. Finally, mean+std over time collapses [T×128] into one clip vector — the single point in latent space all probes and geometry operate on.

Scope note: all figures use EnCodec-24k (conv codec, local context). WavLM's pictures would differ in one deep way — its transformer gives every frame global context, so even a local glitch can perturb distant frames. Same [T, D] contract, different physics of spread.
Generated from real latents on 2026-08-21 (RTX 5070, frozen facebook/encodec_24khz). Companions: FIELD_GUIDE.html (the project, zoomed) · MATH_BRUSHUP.html (the math, with videos).
